title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER LX
enhanced_title: The Reckoning: Elizabeth and Mr. Darcy Debate Love's Origins and Future Fortunes
author: Jane Austen
description: In Chapter 60 of Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth and Mr. Darcy recount the origins of their love, exchange letters with family members, and look forward to life at Pemberley amidst the comedic social discomforts of courtship.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's playful inquiry into what first attracted Darcy to her is one of the novel's most revealing exchanges. Her question—'How could you begin?'—signals a new freedom in their relationship, one in which she can tease without cruelty and he can confess without pride. The scene demonstrates how their engagement has transformed mutual antagonism into genuine intimacy, allowing both characters to revisit their shared history with warmth rather than defensiveness.

Darcy's admission that he cannot fix on 'the hour, or the spot, or the look, or the words' that laid the foundation of his love is among the most psychologically honest moments in the novel. His confession that 'I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun' suggests that love, for him, was not a deliberate choice but an imperceptible accumulation. This stands in sharp contrast to his earlier pride and rationalism, marking the depth of his transformation.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
I was in the middle before I
knew that I _had_ begun.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's theory that Darcy was 'sick of civility, of deference, of officious attention' is a brilliant piece of social analysis delivered with characteristic wit. She identifies the mechanism of his attraction—her difference from the women who courted his approval—and frames it as a compliment to his underlying character. Her conclusion, 'To be sure you know no actual good of me—but nobody thinks of that when they fall in love,' is both self-deprecating and philosophically astute, acknowledging the irrational nature of romantic attachment.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
To be sure you know no actual good of me--but nobody thinks
of _that_ when they fall in love.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The irony of Lady Catherine's role in the lovers' union is savored by Elizabeth with characteristic wit. Darcy confirms that his aunt's 'unjustifiable endeavours to separate us were the means of removing all my doubts,' making her interference the very catalyst that secured the engagement. Elizabeth's observation that 'Lady Catherine has been of infinite use, which ought to make her happy, for she loves to be of use' transforms an act of hostility into a comic gift, underscoring Austen's mastery of ironic reversal.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Lady Catherine has been of infinite use, which ought to make her happy,
for she loves to be of use.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Darcy's disclosure that his real purpose in coming to Netherfield was 'to see you, and to judge, if I could, whether I might ever hope to make you love me' reveals the vulnerability beneath his composed exterior. His secondary avowed purpose—to assess Jane's feelings for Bingley—demonstrates that his sense of responsibility toward his friend persisted even as his own romantic hopes were uncertain. The dual motivation shows a man capable of holding private longing and social duty simultaneously, a mark of genuine moral growth.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
My real purpose was to see _you_, and to judge, if I could, whether I
might ever hope to make you love me.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter's survey of congratulatory letters offers a precise social taxonomy of sincerity. Miss Bingley's congratulations are described as 'all that was affectionate and insincere,' while Georgiana's joy fills four sides of paper with earnest desire to be loved by her new sister. The contrast is pointed: Austen uses the epistolary form not merely as plot mechanism but as a moral register, distinguishing those who feel from those who merely perform feeling.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Miss Bingley’s congratulations to her brother on his approaching
marriage were all that was affectionate and insincere.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter's closing reflection on the 'uncomfortable feelings arising from all this' social exposure is quietly profound. Elizabeth endures the vulgarity of Mrs. Philips and the obsequious flattery of Sir William Lucas on Darcy's behalf, shielding him as best she can. The narrator's observation that these discomforts 'added to the hope of the future' transforms present embarrassment into anticipatory pleasure, and the vision of 'all the comfort and elegance of their family party at Pemberley' becomes the chapter's emotional destination.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
though the uncomfortable feelings
arising from all this took from the season of courtship much of its
pleasure, it added to the hope of the future; and she looked forward
with delight to the time when they should be removed from society so
little pleasing to either, to all the comfort and elegance of their
family party at Pemberley.

summary: Chapter 60 of Pride and Prejudice presents Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy in intimate conversation, teasing out the origins of their affection and recounting the events that led to their engagement. Elizabeth playfully questions Darcy about what first attracted him to her, leading to his famous admission that he 'was in the middle before I knew that I had begun.' Their exchange reveals their intellectual compatibility and the genuine transformation of their relationship from mutual disdain to deep affection. The chapter then follows their correspondence with various family members: Elizabeth writes joyfully to Mrs. Gardiner, Mr. Bennet composes a characteristically sarcastic letter to Mr. Collins, and Darcy prepares his announcement to Lady Catherine. The narrative contrasts sincere reactions—Georgiana's exuberant happiness, Jane's kind but knowing response—with Miss Bingley's 'affectionate and insincere' congratulations. The chapter concludes with Elizabeth anticipating their escape to Pemberley, finding in their current social discomforts at Longbourn evidence of the happiness that awaits them in their future life together.
